title: The United States of Propaganda
gist: Susan Neiman argues American voters mislabel the absence of social rights as 'affordability' or 'inflation' because they lack the vocabulary for anything else — and cites Gallup showing 66% of Democrats view socialism favorably versus 42% for capitalism, Mamdani's New York mayoralty, and 57% of U.S. teenagers naming 'influencer' as their dream job as markers of a leftward shift establishment politics is misreading.

insights.claim: American voters lacking the concept of social rights describe the resulting precarity as a lack of 'affordability' or 'inflation' — meaning the affordability political frame is a proxy for a structural grievance monetary policy cannot fix.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Falling CPI will not defuse the affordability politics driving policy — expect continued redistributive and price-control pressure even in a disinflationary environment.
insights.quote: voters call their unhappiness a lack of “affordability” or “inflation.”
insights.locator: Those who watch this sort of thing regularly

insights.claim: In the U.S., fear of losing your job is coupled to fear of losing your home and health insurance — a bundling Americans feel but do not recognize as abnormal by international standards.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Employment-linked benefits amplify the economic and political consequences of layoffs in the U.S. relative to peers — a reason U.S. consumer sentiment is more sensitive to labor-market wobbles.
insights.quote: In the United States, fear of losing your job is connected to the fear of losing your home and your health insurance. Americans know this in their bones. What they don’t know is that it isn’t normal.

insights.claim: A social right is categorically different from a benefit or a safety net: benefits are granted by the grace of the powerful and safety nets presuppose a fall, and both imply humiliation — the sign of what Avishai Margalit called an indecent society.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: A useful distinction for reading welfare-policy debates: framing determines whether a program is politically durable (a right) or perpetually cuttable (a benefit).
insights.quote: A social right is neither a benefit nor a safety net.
insights.locator: A social right is neither a benefit

insights.claim: The 1948 U.N. Declaration of Human Rights listed fair labor practices, education, housing, healthcare and access to culture as rights alongside political rights, and the United States specifically did not want social rights included.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: U.S. exceptionalism on social rights is a deliberate historical choice, not an accident — meaning convergence toward European models would require an explicit political reversal.
insights.locator: But what if healthcare, parental and sick leave

insights.claim: FDR's 1944 State of the Union proposed a second U.S. Bill of Rights covering employment paying enough for adequate food, clothing and recreation, a decent home, medical care and education — establishing that the U.S. once had a mainstream social-rights tradition.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Provides historical legitimacy that current U.S. left movements can invoke, lowering the political cost of social-rights proposals.

insights.claim: Gallup found in September 2025 that 66 percent of U.S. Democrats had a favorable view of socialism while only 42 percent said the same about capitalism.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: A 24-point gap inside one of two major parties is a hard indicator that redistributive and anti-corporate policy has a durable constituency — price political risk for high-margin, concentrated industries.
insights.quote: According to Gallup, in September 2025, 66 percent of U.S. Democrats had a favorable view of socialism; only 42 percent say the same about capitalism.
insights.locator: In the United States and elsewhere, enthusiasm for socialism

insights.claim: Zohran Mamdani — described as a figure who would be considered a centrist social democrat in most of the world — became New York City's mayor despite many Democrats declining to endorse him and depicting him as a savage communist.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Establishment opposition failed to stop a left-populist in the largest U.S. city — a template other candidates will copy, with implications for municipal tax, housing and rent policy.

insights.claim: Anti-communism is more powerful in the U.S. today than during the McCarthy-era Red Scare because homegrown socialist movements then gave Americans real socialist neighbors, preventing the word from being purely a demonized abstraction.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Explains the intensity of establishment backlash to left candidates — the rhetorical tools are strong but, as Mamdani shows, increasingly ineffective at the ballot box.
insights.quote: While that Red Scare ruined more lives (so far), it was less totalitarian when homegrown socialist movements existed.

insights.claim: Hannah Arendt's insight that rage arises only where there is reason to suspect conditions could be changed and are not explains why U.S. political anger is rising now rather than during earlier, more muffled periods of inequality.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Visible alternatives, not absolute deprivation, drive political volatility — social media exposure to elite consumption is the accelerant.
insights.quote: Only where there is reason to suspect that conditions could be changed and are not does rage arise.

themes.theme: Labor conditions and the influencer economy

insights.claim: U.S. railway companies cut their workforce by 30 percent, leaving remaining workers required to be available day and night and to appear within 90 minutes if called — the real grievance behind the 2022 strike threat by 115,000 workers.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Extreme labor-cost optimization in rail creates recurring strike risk and single-point-of-failure exposure in U.S. freight — an operational risk for shippers.

insights.claim: In the 2022 rail dispute, workers settled for a 14 percent pay increase; Biden sought seven days of annual sick leave against the unions' demand for 14, and the Senate rejected it and offered one day per year.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that U.S. labor gains come as wages rather than conditions — pay-driven settlements keep inflation pressure up while leaving structural grievance unresolved.

insights.claim: 57 percent of U.S. teenagers name 'influencer' as their dream profession even though earnings cannot support the average single influencer, let alone one with a family.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: A generational labor-supply signal: aspiration is concentrating in a winner-take-all market with negligible median income, implying persistent underemployment and platform dependence.
insights.quote: When asked about their dream profession, 57 percent of U.S. teenagers name “influencer.”
insights.locator: In earlier eras, barring an occasional peasant rebellion

insights.claim: Social media brings elite consumption directly into ordinary homes, converting what was once distant inequality into a daily reminder of what followers lack — and conspicuous consumption is no longer treated as a term of critique.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Platform-mediated inequality visibility is a structural driver of political instability in developed markets, independent of actual income trends.
insights.locator: In earlier eras, barring an occasional peasant rebellion

insights.claim: Propaganda is hardest to detect where media are private and formal censorship is absent, and part of the propaganda of self-described liberal democracies is the claim that they do not allow propaganda.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: A reason to treat consensus narratives in Western media as information with systematic omissions rather than as neutral baseline — comparative sourcing is the corrective.
insights.quote: Part of the propaganda of states that consider themselves liberal democracies is that they do not allow propaganda.
insights.locator: This is especially true when the media portray themselves

insights.claim: Bias in news becomes visible only through side-by-side comparison of opposing sources — listening to East and West Berlin radio revealed each side's omissions in a way neither alone could.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: A practical analytical method: read adversarial sources in parallel specifically to detect what each omits, not to average their claims.
insights.quote: only repeated comparisons made that clear
insights.locator: East Berlin radio offered credible information

insights.claim: The U.S. infant mortality rate is higher than Belarus's or Cuba's, and U.S. students perform below the OECD average in math and around average in reading and science despite higher per-student spending than most developed countries.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Poor outcomes per dollar in U.S. health and education is a persistent productivity drag and the empirical core of the political case for structural reform.

insights.claim: Greg Grandin's judgment is cited that no comparable nation presided over such an enormous upward redistribution of wealth after the Cold War, creating a superclass of billionaires immune to democratic control.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Concentration of wealth beyond democratic reach is precisely the target of rising left politics — a long-run tax and regulatory risk for large fortunes and their holding structures.
insights.quote: No other comparable nation … presided over such an enormous redistribution of wealth upwards, creating a superclass of billionaires immune to democratic control.

insights.claim: Bismarck introduced German state health insurance in 1883 specifically to blunt rising socialism, and per Gary Gerstle the threat of communism gave capitalist countries a reason to improve workers' lives — with no competing system since 1990, European social rights have been cut back.
insights.speaker: Susan Neiman
insights.so_what: Welfare provision historically responds to organized systemic threat; the rise of a credible left electoral bloc is the modern analogue that could reverse three decades of retrenchment.
insights.quote: the threat of communism provided a reason for capitalist countries to improve workers’ lives
